projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Dale Kuhlman was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Mr. Kuhlman, let's begin with your birthplace, where you were raised, where you went to school and we'll move on to your Service time and then your post Service time and in your case, we'll talk about your second tour of duty.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Very well. I was born in Pemberville, Ohio on a farm near Scotch Ridge, New Rochester. I graduated from Webster High School in 1934. I wanted to go to college so that I wanted to be a teacher, a school teacher and a coach, so I went to Bowling Green University. That was the college then, the state teacher's college. I didn't have much money on this 80-acre farm. We always had enough to eat but not much money, so I worked my way through Bowling Green. I drove back and forth from the farm when I was a freshman but then in the sophomore, junior, senior year, I made the athletic teams and since I was interested in coaching, I stayed at, in Bowling Green so that I could participate in the athletics. I graduated from Bowling Green in 1938. I did make letters in football, basketball and baseball which helped me get a job when I graduated. I got a job in Wayne, Ohio. I remember I, one of the fortunate few to get a job for $1,200 a year. I had a full teaching load and coached football, basketball and baseball. Luckily, we were very successful that first year. We won the county championship in football, basketball and track so that they thought I was a pretty good coach and was offered some jobs in the area, one of which was Perrysburg, Ohio, so I moved to Perrysburg, Ohio in 1939 and coached and taught school until Pearl Harbor. I went in the next day, the next morning, told the superintendent that I would teach till the end of the semester and then join the Navy, which I did. After a basketball game in Perrysburg, I drove to Chicago, I remember on Route 6 on a foggy night in a 1940 Chevrolet and interviewed with Gene Tunny who had been a boxer but he was recruiting for the Navy. Interviewed with him and he said if you go through boots in Norfolk, Virginia and survive that, we'll give you chief petty officer's rating which interested me. I think I could have waited and gotten a commission direct because in college I joined the National Guard. I made a buck a night, I remember, as a buck private, Company L, 148th Infantry 37th Division. A dollar would buy me four meals, 25 cents a meal so that I did have some military time when I was in college. Kind of interesting, I made private first class and got $1.10 but then I had a basketball game on Tuesday night when I was supposed to drill and I missed drill. I got busted back from $1.10 PFC back to a buck again, but I gained that back eventually. But that's how it was in those days, you needed a doctor's slip in order to miss drill. But I did then enlist in the Navy and went through boots at Norfolk, Virginia. There were many athletes, coaches and professional athletes there and it was a pretty tough boot camp but I survived that and stayed there on the staff for a while and then was sent to a radio school in Madison, Wisconsin at the University of Wisconsin which was good duty, actually. I could have stayed there a longer time but I didn't feel that I wanted to spend my whole Navy career at a university radio school, so I put in for a commission and was appointed ensign so that I left the University of Wisconsin as a chief, went to school at Gulfport, Mississippi. It was an armed guard school. We took gunnery and airplane identification, communications and I was probably there at Gulfport, Mississippi for a couple of months and then from there transferred, was asked to go to New Orleans and wait assignment aboard an armed guard ship. Armed guard, you may or may not know, is, I was in charge of a gun crew. We had three-inch/.50 forward on this Liberty ship, five-eighth/.38 aft. We had four .20 millimeters on the bridge and 27 men gun crew and it was our duty to defend the ship in case of attack or prevent Germans or whomever from boarding our ship and taking over. The merchant crew actually ran the ship. They were in charge and there were about I think 50 men. It was kind of a problem not especially on my ship but the merchant crew made a lot of money. They had to pay them a lot of money in order to get them on those ships because it was hazardous duty. A little Spanish-American man that took care of my quarters, and I was an ensign or JG at the time, probably or ensign, he made more money than I did. My men made maybe $50 a month and he made probably 500, so that that was a bone of contention in Liberty ships in the Navy in those days, but we got along. From New Orleans I was sent to Houston, Texas to pick up a Liberty ship, and think the name was Rufus Choate, a new Liberty ship made by Todd Shipyards in Houston, so I was there on the shake-down crews and I was assigned 27 men on my ship and it's, as I recall, it's a long time ago but we loaded this new ship on the way up to New York and we carried everything from beans to bullets they said. We went to New York and then joined up with a convoy. We had the meeting of the Navy and the commanders of these convoys and perhaps there were 30 or 40 ships in this convoy. We were given a number and maybe they had five abreast and say six deep, that would be 30 ships all loaded, most of them Liberty ships. They were very slow, 10, 12 knots but we actually built a bridge to Britain. Really, if it hadn't been for those Liberty ships and those type ships, I don't think England would have survived; but my, most of my trips were fairly uneventful. We took the northern route normally. In good weather, it was comfortable but in bad weather, and you got a lot of bad weather in that northern shipway, it was foggy, cold, miserable, rough and you were supposed to keep some semblance of order in that convoy but at night we'd drag a fog buoy and try and follow that so we could follow the ship in front of us and we'd drag a ship behind, a buoy behind us so it was I guess somewhat hazardous duty. Early in the war, there were a lot of German submarines in the area. We had Navy destroyers or destroyer escorts going around our convoy trying to keep us in some semblance of order, but after a couple of days of bad weather, you'd, in the morning when it cleared up, you'd see ships all over the horizon and then we'd catch hell for not being in proper position and we'd try to get back in position and eventually came in the North Channel usually and as I recall we came into Liverpool quite often. That seemed to be the way most of the convoys were going but you can imagine, you know, 30 ships, each ship probably carried how many carloads of equipment and supplies that really we dumped into Britain and as a result of that, Britain was I think able to defend themselves and survive. On one occasion we unloaded, as I recall, in Liverpool and then went into the Mediterranean, went through the canal or the channel and shuttled from Algers, North Africa into Marcais, France hauling equipment, material back and forth. That was kind of monotonous. We finally ran out of food and supplies and came back to New York. I think that was one of our, one of our last trips there and came back to New York on VE Day which was quite a surprise and celebration. Spent some time then celebrating and I think I got a leave and went on home for a week or ten days probably. In the meantime, I was married. My wife stayed back and taught school briefly while I was gone, and then --

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: I'd like to ask you some questions --

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Yeah, go ahead.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: -- that have come up. You mentioned that you had a convoy of 30 to 40 ships?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: And you had a destroyer escort. Did you ever come under U-boat attack?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Well, we didn't directly. Our convoy did, but we didn't know for sure who was survived and who was sunk but the weather was so rough, I remember one time and I just happened to think of this, the ship beside of us had a large locomotive tied on the top deck. Well, it was rough. Pretty soon that locomotive started to move an inch, pretty soon banged back and forth and the locomotive went over the side, so the whole thing; but early in the war German U-boats were a threat. They said early in the war 95 percent of those German sailors on U-boats came back. At the end of the war, five percent.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: So there was a big change there in a few years.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Did you have any air protection part of the way or --

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Yes, part of the way. Out of New York, part of the way and then part of the way, but not quite all the way, as I recall --

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Yes, so there was --

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: -- on those ships.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: -- that spot in between there where you were without air protection and I suppose that's where the sub, the subs were?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Well, I think that's right. We didn't have air protection all the way.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: And were they, were the submarines moving in wolfpacks at that time?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Yes. Not early in the war, as I recall, they weren't; but near the end of the war, there were wolfpacks. One of the problems if you were sunk, sailors got in the water, you couldn't drop your depth charges because of the concussion.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: You'd kill your own people, so --

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: And you were never sunk, but did you see ships sunk?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: No, not directly. We had groomers that so, one of them got hit and some --

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: -- but I didn't get hit and I didn't actually see it. I did see some activity, but nothing that I was involved in.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Were these ships you were on considered very seaworthy?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Well, those Liberty ships were kind of a temporary ship. Kaiser built most of them and some of them broke in two. They, in rough weather, they were riveted but they'd get a crack in there and they had to send them back to make them much safer because not all of them survived in rough weather but it was a reciprocal engine, 10, 12 knots so the convoy was slow but we got there with the material by the hundreds of ships; but if it hadn't been for the Liberty ships, I don't think that England would have survived because we just took tons and tons of, carloads of things.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Well, I spent a month on a Liberty ship crossing the ocean both ways and, you know --

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Well, good for you. I hope you had a rough ride.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: -- it was a scary experience for me, so that's why I'm asking you about that.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Well, yeah, some of them, they carried troops. They had some that could carry some troops. We carried -- well, they had five holds as the ship goes and heavily loaded. They would take a lot of cargo, but I don't think there are any of them left anymore, at --

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Did you come under air attract at all?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Our convoy did but I did not. We didn't fire our guns.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: You didn't, but --

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: -- so you were spread out all over the ocean?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Well, that's right. Normally you're supposed to stay in line and stay in some semblance of order but when you can't see and you can't communicate, we used fog horns. We used fog buoys and kind of felt our way over across the ocean.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Did you maintain radio contact at all?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Well, there was silence sometimes because you couldn't, you had a signalman aboard and they had a ship radioman. Sometimes you'd get emergency turn, a 45 degree turn, you know, to port. Well, some of these young seamen went starboard and then in the middle of the convoy, you'd see them bumping their way out of there and some people wrecked their own ships because of inexperience, but it was, it was interesting duty but not really aboard a Navy ship as such. A lot of people don't realize the armed guard, I don't think, what we did back then.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Oh, I think that's a -- as far as the number of interviews I have done to date, which is about 75, I have never spoken to anyone who had such duty as you had.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: So each interview is a new experience for me.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Well, I think a lot of the officers were selected because they had been school teachers or they had been in athletics. You had to get along with the merchant crew. You had to get -- you were the only officer, Navy officer and you had to get along with your men, kind of the buffer between the maritime and the Navy.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: When you said that the merchant marines, seamen made far more money than you did?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Were they, were they volunteers?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Well, they had to pay a lot of money to get them on those ships. They paid them -- they were volunteers pretty much. They joined the merchants -- they went to maritime school, the officers went to maritime school, but the seamen, ordinary seamen just signed on because they made pretty good money, but my Navy boys I think he were getting $50 a month and, I don't know, I was getting as an ensign maybe 120 or something thereabouts, I don't know, but I had noplace to spend it. You know, I saved it.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: It didn't matter.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: You couldn't spend it.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: So they were volunteers and they were paid far more, far better than you were?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Oh, sure.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: And --

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: And you were sort of impressed into service?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Well, yeah --

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: I guess --

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: -- I went where the Navy told me to go.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Yes. You have to.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: I went and I survived and thought I did my fair share.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Now, you mentioned the northern route. What is the northern route?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Well, the great circle, the great northern, way up north. For some reason, they say it's shorter.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Oh, just like they fly today, through --

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Yes. They fly that way, so we usually took that, even though it was the bad weather and, but normally it was up to the convoy commodore pretty much. If he got word that there was submarine packs ahead, we'd divert and go a different direction.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: But --

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: So then you traveled back and forth, did you, between --

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Basically New York and Liverpool.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: And Liverpool. Liverpool was an important harbor?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: That way you didn't have to come into the English Channel?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: That's right. We come in the North Channel as I recall.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Yeah, I suppose the English Channel was very busy with U-boats.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Well, I think so, but then we went -- yeah, that's right -- to Lieberburg, I remember the Lieberburg was on top of a building, Lieberburg at Liverpool and then a place called Blackpool.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: That was a pretty good place for Liberty.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: I remember going to Blackpool for Liberty.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: That's where the big amusement park is.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Yes. Well, you seem to know.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Well, you know maybe more about it than I do.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: So then your main function then was to protect ships traveling back and forth across carrying supplies?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Yes. Now, early in the war, I, if merchant crews didn't have any guns, you know, the Germans could surface and take over your ship or sink you from the surface, which happened early in the war.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Now, did you also have, in these convoys, destroyer escorts or destroyer --

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Yes, we had destroyer escorts most of the way. They'd circle around and try to keep you in some sem -- like a mother hen, to keep you in line.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Now, so in all of your duty in World War II, then, you've never, you never came under attack?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Not directly. I saw the, was it the U -- oh, the not U-boats, U -- that they'd fly. What'd they call them? I don't know. They flew over the Mediterranean late in the war. The Germans had them, the --

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Oh, the Rockets?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: The Rockets.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: I forget what they're called.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: The V, V bombs?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: V bomb Rockets. They had so much gas, when they'd run out --

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Yeah. Then they'd drop --

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: They'd drop, they wouldn't know exactly where but in the area of London.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: I see. And did you spend time in England at, while you were there?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Yes, when they were loading and unloading.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Did you get to London?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Not that, I've been to London since then but I didn't when I was in the Navy.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: So you were not there to see the destruction of the --

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: -- of the V bombs?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: And the Battle of Britain?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: No, but I met British people and went to some of their functions in Liverpool and had a good experience there, I think.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: How were you treated by the Brits?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Very, very fine. Of course they were short of, you know, they didn't have a lot of food. We tried to give them a little food off our ship and people we'd meet and try to help them.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: And what did you, what was your cargo on these Liberty ships?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Oh, boy, I don't, you know, they said from beans to bullets, whatever. It just varied every time. We carried ammunition sometimes; but I don't really know, I wasn't unloading and loading, so I, we had our own booms, we could load and unload without assistance of other ships, so they'd work day and night around the clock on those.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Well, what was the elapsed time that generally from New York to Liverpool?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Oh, boy, I think that sometimes took us a couple weeks, ten days. Depends on the weather and the route.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: But the convoy had to go slow, as slow as the slowest ship.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Because you didn't like to be a straggler. If you were a straggler out by yourself, you were a sitting duck for the submarines.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: It has been said that if your ship were sunk in a convoy, that the other ships could not stop to pick you up?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: I think that's right. They'd keep going.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: So if you were alive in the water, you were --

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: They couldn't dilly-dally around to subject themselves to more attack.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: So the merchant seamen were at great risk?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Yes, yes. They were. That's why they had to pay them. Some got a hundred percent bonus in certain areas as I recall, certain areas that were hazardous, they'd get a good bonus.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Probably up in that Vermanscrund (ph)?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Oh, that Vermanscrund (ph), I thought we were going to go there but about half of them didn't make it.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Yes, and that was --

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Oh, I didn't want to go there.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Now, there if you got in the water, that was certain death, wasn't it?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: I think so --

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: From hypothermia.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: -- and it was bad early in the war. We were insulated. I was thinking we might go there. We could have but we, luckily we didn't, and --

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: How many trips would you guess you made back and forth?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Oh, I didn't make I guess only about four trips because I got in a little bit late. I was a chief petty officer, you know, at this radio school and then this assignment. I was an ensign then I think or JG, junior grade, but I had a good crew and we got along well. It was a good experience.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Did you and your crew move as a unit from ship to ship?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: A few of us. You mean if I got another ship, I got a little different crew because they'd go home on leave, and --

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: -- to other assignments, but my gunner's mate I tried to keep with me at all times.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: And where were you when the war in Europe ended?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Well, this is interesting. I was back in New York VE Day, I got to go home and I thought well, maybe, you know, maybe I wouldn't have to go but then I was sent back to New Orleans and picked up another ship, was loaded and went through the canal and we were going to go to Lai Tai which would have taken 40 days and 40 nights, I think. It was a long ways, but we loaded, heavily loaded, went through the canal. I think it was June 1st, 1945. I was up on the bridge until midnight, saw a ship coming towards the canal as we were going out. The second mate was on watch. I went down to my quarters and hadn't been down there over a half-hour, 45 minutes, the general alarm rang. I grabbed my flashlight, lifejacket, ran up the ladder and, whoom, I thought we were torpedoed. We had a head-on collision with another ship and I was concerned, the bow of that ship went right through the quarters of my Navy people but I could get on the sound part phones and all my guys had reported to their gun stations. The merchant crew didn't respond and they were crushed, some of them were killed. I think about four of them were killed but military discipline saved the life of -- {cough} I can hardly talk about it, but --

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Now, this was also --

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: -- a Liberty ship?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: It was a Liberty com -- it was a Greek Liberty coming in. It was a meeting situation. Had we gone straight ahead, we'd have missed miles probably, you know, but these second mates, inexperienced, well, that's a meeting situation, the guy coming in said oh, I'd better hold her starboard like you would on a road. Our mate said, oh, boy, he's still on my right, a little bit on the starboard, I'll hold her port. So it was kind of a fight; port, starboard, starboard, port, port, starboard. It came out even and wham.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: And where was this?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Well, it was just outside of Panama in the Pacific, but --

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: So you were getting, you were just going out and --

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: We were heading --

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: -- he was just coming in.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: He was coming in and we were going out.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: But my man on watch rang the general alarm so it was inevitable it was going to hit. He didn't -- well, they rang it soon enough, but they could have rung it a little bit sooner but I had been teaching and coaching and timing these guys. Sometimes I'd ring the alarm and give them hell for not getting there sooner which maybe they didn't like, but it saved their life. They got up to their gun quarters. Then the merchant crew took all the lifeboats because we were going down, the decks were washed, they took the lifeboats so I didn't have much left for my guys, I had rafts, so I said, "Okay. Abandon ship in the rafts," so they got in the rafts. I said, "Get away from the ship as far as you can," the rope, the line they call it, "stay away but if she goes down, make sure you pull the toggle pin because it will pull you down with it," and it was warm and calm. The radio man, the captain and I stayed aboard. I had my lifejacket on. I wasn't going to go down with the ship but my guys said, "Lieutenant, don't go down with the ship. Let us come in and get you. We'll come in and get you." You know, I said, "No. I'm all right. Just stay away from the ship. Now, be sure if she goes down you --" "Well, don't get in the water. There's sharks out there." I said, "Those are porpoise." "Oh, they'll rip you to death." Well, we just didn't know if we were going to sink or swim but we kept afloat and the next morning, then, daylight, I had the guys come back aboard and we were carrying pontoons and landing barges. We had landing barges lashed down because we were heading for Japan and I called my gunner's mate and said, "Gunner, I think this thing's full of gas. See if this thing will run." He turned it on, boom, it started right now and it was full of gas, so I said, "Hey, listen, here's our lifeboat if this thing sinks, let's unlash this thing." So we threw our valuables in this thing and we unbuckled it so if we'd have gone down, I think it would have been on and we could have run that thing back to Panama but the next day then they sent a tug out. The tug was too small. He just buttonhooked, he couldn't pull us, it was too heavy on the right, on the starboard side, so I remember I had Coca-Cola in my room, several cases of Coke and we found cans of salmon, so I gave the Coca-Cola to my guys and we opened the cans of salmon so we had Coke and we drank Coke and ate salmon for a couple days until we got back to Panama.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: What happened to the ship then?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Well, it was beyond repair. They took the bodies out and all the meat and all the, everything out and it was beyond repair, so --

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: So then you got another ship --

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: But that was --

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: -- and continued on?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Yes. I thought maybe we'd get survivor's leave or something because we helped take up the tugs and, you know.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: And the ship that hit you?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Well, he was hit in the bow. He went bow down, but his propellers and engine room wasn't injured at all so he, we were stuck together for a while. He finally broke loose and then I was afraid, you know, there was oil and sparks and ammunition but nothing happened. He broke loose and he went in on his own and left us out there but then the tugs came eventually, but that was kind of exciting for, but then I stayed aboard the ship in the dry dock. They wanted me to stay aboard because the Panamanians were stealing everything off there so I kept eight men from my crew to stand guard day and night for a while and I stayed on the ship. It wasn't fit to stay on but I stayed on it for a while and then got acquainted with an Army flier and flew with him over Costa Rica and had a little experience there. I played golf. I couldn't do much. Then there was a hearing, of course, and I had to testify. Well, both mates lost their license. Our mate should have called the captain right away, you know, like they do in the Navy but, we had a good captain but he was asleep. It was 1:00 in the morning and he wasn't up there. He was 72 years old. He was an older gentleman, a nice gentleman that had a lot of experience but this mate, you know, hard port and the other one hard starboard and it came out even and it was a disaster.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: What about the LSTs for Lai Tai?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Well, they unloaded us and I don't know what happened to them, put them on another --

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: You did not then continue on to Lai Tai?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: No, I stayed around there for a couple of months. In fact, I stayed there -- this happened in June and I was there yet in August when they dropped the atomic bomb.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: So you were there in Panama for VJ -- END OF SIDE ONE, TAPE ONE. BEGIN SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: For the atomic bomb and then I was assigned a tanker and then I went to Eniwetok and Kwajalein.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Oh, I see. So you --

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Still, the war was about over but they assigned me another ship and I took that one to Eniwetok and Kwajalein and came back to Panama.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Were the Japanese subs or the -- active or were the Kamikazes active?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: No, not that late in the war. {TAPE RECORDER TURNED OFF.}

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Well, I was in Panama, as I said, when they dropped the atomic bomb and then of course I think the Japanese surrendered shortly thereafter. I was assigned a tanker with a small crew, maybe on a nine man gun crew and went to Eniwetok and Kwajalein and unloaded and came back to Panama and whether it was that same tanker, I was sent back then aboard a different ship. I think it was a transport and I was kind of surprised, I got a message to throw all the ammunition overboard and I read and reread that and wanted to be sure I was doing the right thing, but I guess I was and did and we threw a lot of ammunition then overboard on the way back to States, just about everything, I think on that ship, all the ammunition was thrown overboard and I came back then to the States and was sent to Chicago Separation Center and from Chicago they sent me to Toledo to get out of the military and the captain, the commander, I think he was a full commander, said to me, "I need a ship's service officer here. You teach school. School's in session now. Would you stay on and be my ship's service officer here at this separation center?" I said, "Well, yes, if you think I can do it. I have not had much experience running a store." "Well," he says, "you can do it." So I stayed on and stayed until the separation center here in Toledo was closed but that was a good experience for me, running this store, the men were paid off and they bought a lot of supplies, jewelry and rings and all sorts of things and evidently, I did a pretty good job because the captain says, "Kuhlman, you're doing a good job, you're making too much money down there." He says, "We have to send this all back to Washington, D.C., the money goes back there and I don't want to send them the money." He said, "You know, give it to some of the boys here. Don't be greedy." So I then lost money intentionally. I remember we were, bought sandwiches from Buddy's Box Lunch, who was --

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: -- here in Toledo and bought them, I think maybe paid 20 cents and was probably selling them for 25. I said, "Well, let's sell those for 10 cents" but, and Virg Gladio from Buddy's came out there and he said, "Lieutenant, you could speed this line up a little bit. You could have a line here and a line there and you can speed this up. They wouldn't have to wait in line so long." And I said, "Virg, I'm losing money fast enough." He said, "What do you mean?" I said, "Look. I'm selling this stuff for less money than I paid you for it." "Oh, my God," he said, "I've never seen that before in my life," but I stayed there and helped close that up and he give me kind of a spot promotion, the commander did, and I made lieutenant commander then and then came back in '46, could have taught school at DeVilbiss in Toledo or Perrysburg or different places. I thought I wanted to get into industry because they were paying a little bit more money and I made connections with Libbey-Owens-Ford when I was in Perrysburg teaching and coaching so then I went with Libbey-Owens in '46 as assistant to the personnel director and then made assistant personnel director and then made corporate personnel director before I retired in 1974 but then I didn't, I don't think we mentioned the Korean War here too much.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Oh, we have to get you back into the Service.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Back in the Service a couple more years, huh?

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Well, I stayed in the Reserve, and when you're in the Reserve if they call you, you go; so I was called to Bayonne, New Jersey to report to the naval supply depot, Bayonne, New Jersey. That must have been in -- well, the Korean War was 1952, I guess, I went in. Got out in '53. I was in about two years, but he asked me to be safety, security and safety officer. Safety came under my department at Libbey-Owens-Ford, so I had some experience and he said I'd be in charge of the fire department -- we had a big fire department, about 30 men, I think -- police department, Marines and it was a good experience. I was in charge of that whole naval supply base for a couple of years and ships come in there to load and unload but there are mostly supply officers there. I was one of the only, about the only line officer, I think, but it worked out quite well. I got a lot of experience that helped me in my job when I came back to Libbey-Owens-Ford. Fire prevention, and I remember when I came back to Libbey-Owens-Ford walking through one of the plants, I said, "This plant's a fire hazard," and I think it was. I talked to the manager, plant manager and I said, "You know, I'm afraid to walk through this plant. You got oil, you got guys getting, your hoses aren't safe, your fire extinguishers aren't charged up. We got to do something about this. If you have a fire, you're going to lose this plant." He said, "Well, you mentioned it. You take over. You're in charge." So I did and luckily so. We had fire brigade training and things worked out quite well and luckily we had some good firemen that, we had a fire that would have been big fires so that my experience there at the naval supply depot carried over with Libbey-Owens-Ford when I came back and they realized it and then were good to me; so actually my Navy experience helped me with my job here although they didn't like it when I left for a couple of years again, you know.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Well, that's an interesting question. When you went in the Service, you had a certain job. When you went back in, I should say.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Was that job held for you?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: My job at Libbey-Owens-Ford was held for me. Oh, yes. They had to, but --

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: That was a requirement?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Yes, but they didn't like it too well that I left.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: When you returned, you went --

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: I had my job back.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: -- back to your old job and perhaps --

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: But I don't know if I, at first I didn't get the promotions that I probably would have gotten.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: But I did later after, things worked out all right.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: So but generally American industry operated that way during America's wars?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Yes, but way back early in the war, some of those companies didn't like it too well if you were gone and had an important job with them, they were, you know, self, they were part of themselves first but I, they treated me fairly and I treated them I think fairly but I was gone a couple of years, you know --

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: -- in that era.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Whoever took your spot had to know that he was in a temporary position?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: And he was perhaps not too happy with that prospect?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Well, no, but he, he did all right. See, employment came under my job, employment, safety, Workmen's Comp, recreation and all of those, so it worked out pretty well.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Now, were you involved, you a part of the, you said you were involved with the naval armory out there?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: And it is closing now?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Is that a bone of contention with the, with Navy or ex-Navy personnel?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Well, I haven't followed it very close but I can't understand, it looks like they were going to sell it for less money than they could get for it and I don't understand why. There must be some politics behind it someplace. I don't know what it is and maybe we shouldn't say, but -- and I'm not an authority on it, but I, that was a pretty nice building. I went there every Monday night to drill and on weekends and it was a, it was kept up well. That's a nice, big wooden floor and I guess it's deteriorated since. Of course that's been years ago when I left there.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: So the Navy had no, had no further use for it?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: I don't think so.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: There weren't enough Navy personnel passing through this area to --

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: I don't -- no, I don't think so.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: What was the use for a naval armory in the beginning? Why was such a huge building built?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Well, I don't know if they ever filled that. We filled it pretty well with, we had several divisions in training when I was there, but before the war, I don't know what that was used for.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: But you think it was a training facility?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: A training facility. It was a fine old building when I was there. Seemed to be well heated, utilized, parking area, right on the water. Then we had a ship that we could train with and it made a good training facility as I recall. Of course, that's been a long time ago.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: There's another such very large training facility up in the Detroit area also a naval armory up there --

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: -- so perhaps they placed them on waterways to train sailors?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Well, then Selfridge's is also, Selfridge's is up near Detroit. That's right on the water. I think they have Army, Navy, Coast Guard. They have everything, Air Force. They have everything there at Selfridge's and they fly -- as a result of my retirement now, I fly space available or I did, flew space available all over the world several times.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Is that open to everyone?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Well, anyone after you get your retired card.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Oh, I see, you must retire to be --

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: You must be retired to get this card.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: I see, so --

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: So after age -- I was 60. So after age 60 -- I retired from Libbey-Owens-Ford when I was 58 -- my wife and I took a lot of trips all over the world for free. We went to Florida every winter for 25 winters. Went abroad every spring and fall, usually with the military, space available. Met a lot of fine people, and it didn't cost us too much and it was a great experience.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: So I guess in conclusion here, we could say that your military service was a very, very positive thing?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: I think so.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: And --

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Yes, I could -- had I done things over, I probably wouldn't have joined the Navy immediately after Pearl Harbor. I, you know, I quit a $200 a month job for $21 a month and, you know, not too many people would do that. I could of, had I waited, I could have gotten a commission probably and made $100 a month but I didn't.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: But do you believe that your country was properly grateful for your service?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Well, I think so. I, you know, World War II they thought of us different than they did Vietnamese, or Vietnam Veterans but --

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Did you use the GI Bill?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: No, I didn't. Of course I had already had my, I was a little older, see, I had my -- I had graduated and was teaching so I was a little bit older. My brother, now, went in later, a Navy officer, and he was, went through V-12 program but he's since passed away but he used, he went to Harvard, went to Harvard for a year or so, I think. Yep.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Which is --

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Harvard Business School.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: -- absolutely unaffordable.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Oh, yeah. We couldn't, you know, come up with that kind of money.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: But he was a good student and a good athlete and he made commission and he was out in the Pacific. Had it not been for the atomic bomb, I don't know if he would have survived and I don't know that I would have.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: So the general feeling, talking about the atomic bomb, among the Service people was relief?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Oh, sure. It saved our lives, thousands, thousands, hundreds of thousands, I think.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: History today tells us that perhaps a million people might have died in the invasion of Japan, a million including the Japanese and the Americans?

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Yeah. It would have been terrible. It was bad the way it was but it was the lesser of two evils. Oh, yeah, I don't think my brother would have survived and I, I was headed that way, yeah, but, huh, I was thankful for the atomic bomb.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: There is some question about to, you know, some are questioning the use of the bomb.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Well, but I think --

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: But I think the Servicemen are generally agreed, that I have spoken to, are generally agreed that it was a lifesaver for American Servicemen.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Well, the Japanese started it. They bombed Pearl Harbor. What did they want us to do? Turn our back and get killed? We had to fight back. I was in athletics. I was a competitor. {Telephone ringing.}

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: There's somebody calling on the phone, I'll --

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Well, I think we've concluded the interview. It's been very interesting. I've enjoyed it and as I said before, this is the first time I've talked to a person that handled your particular function --

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Well --

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: -- in the Navy, so thank you very much.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: I appreciated the opportunity here and gave the answers to the best of my ability and knowledge but that's been how many years ago.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Well, I think it's typical of the Veterans I've interviewed that their memories of the war, although it was many years ago, are very sharp.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Well, I'm kind of surprised I remembered what I talked about here today. I hadn't really rehearsed it ahead of time, but it's kind of come back to me.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Well, those were very important years of your life.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: And when you think back to it, your memory does become very sharp remembering times and dates.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: But you know at my age now, I'm fortunate to be here and doing as well as I am, I think, and I don't know how many more years I can do it but I'll continue as long as I can, and --

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Well, that's the very function of the Veterans History Project is to talk to Veterans while they're still able to remember and record and leave their memories of the war for posterity.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: My grandchildren would be interested in this tape.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Then we'll get you a copy.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: I'd appreciate that, I would.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Thank you very much.

sp.speaker: Dale Kuhlman
sp.p: Okay. END OF SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE.
